transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I'm here because the clinic for my logistics job wouldn't clear me. They said my weight was too low, which is just ridiculous if you ask me. I mean, to me, I just look lean, you know? Like someone who's ready to work, stay quick on his feet. You have to be quick in freight, otherwise you're just in the way. I remember this one guy, back in '98, big guy, thought he could muscle everything. But he was so slow, tripped over a pallet of dog food and nearly took out the whole racking system. It took us three hours to clean up that mess, and the smell of that dog food... man, it just lingered for days. I can still smell it sometimes when the humidity gets high. But yeah, they said I'm too light to work, which makes no sense.
Do you think your weight is normal?

Well... I mean, my sister and that clinic doctor keep saying I’m in some kind of danger. But they're just making it way bigger than it is. They don’t understand that I’m just keeping myself light, sharp, and ready for work. You gotta be sharp on the floor. 

Just last week, this new kid—barely twenty, I swear—was driving the forklift like an absolute maniac. Came whipping right around the blind corner near the loading docks. If I wasn't light on my feet, he would've pinned me right against the corrugated steel wall. And let me tell you, those steel panels aren't cheap to replace. We had a driver back in 2012 back a whole rig into one of the bay doors, and it took management three months to get the contractor out to fix it. The draft that came through that hole all winter was brutal. We had to wear double thermals just to feel our fingers. My sister was always trying to knit me these thick wool socks back then, but wool just makes my feet sweat in the work boots, and once your boots are wet, you're miserable all shift. 

But yeah, they're just blowing the whole weight thing out of proportion. I'm completely fine.
Are you afraid of gaining weight?

Well, it's not like I'm terrified of it, but... I mean, yeah, I guess I do worry about it. If I eat rice, bread, or something greasy, I can’t stop thinking it will just sit on me right away. I'll be checking the scale or my belt the next morning to make sure I didn’t let myself go. You know how it is, you let your guard down for one second and suddenly everything's out of control. 

Kind of like when they switched our inventory system at the warehouse back in '15. We used to do everything on paper, clipboards and carbon copies. It was a good system, you always had a hard copy if the computers went down. But then corporate brought in these new scanners, said it would make us "more efficient." Half the guys didn't even know how to turn the things on. I remember Jimmy—he was a good guy, retired a few years back, moved down to Florida. He hated the humidity down there, said it ruined his golf swing. But anyway, Jimmy accidentally scanned the same pallet of engine blocks like five times, and the system thought we had enough inventory to supply a whole assembly line. The trucking company sent three extra rigs the next day just to pick up blocks we didn't even have. The logistics manager was screaming so loud his face turned purple. 

But yeah, I just... I check my belt, make sure I'm still tight, still ready to move. You can't afford to get sluggish.
Do you limit what you eat because you're worried about gaining weight?

Well, I guess... yeah, I keep things pretty tight. Most days I just stick to black coffee, maybe a boiled egg or a little bit of tuna. If I'm not actually on the floor moving freight, I just tell myself I don't really need a real meal anyway. You don't need the fuel if the engine ain't running, right? 

Speaking of engines, my buddy Carl—he works over at the auto parts distribution center across town—he was telling me about this whole shipment of alternators they got in last month. Apparently, they were all defective straight from the manufacturer. Just totally shot. Carl said they had to load 'em all back onto the pallets, wrap 'em up, and ship 'em right back to Mexico. The shrink wrap they use over there is garbage, though. It's that thin, cheap stuff that tears if you even look at it funny. I always tell our purchasing guy to buy the heavy-duty wrap, the 80-gauge stuff. It costs a few cents more a roll, but it saves you hours of re-wrapping when a pallet shifts in transit. I remember one time we had a whole skid of windshield washer fluid tip over inside a trailer because some rookie used the cheap wrap. Blue liquid everywhere. Smelled like windex for a month. 

But yeah, I just... I don't eat much. Just keep it light so I don't get weighed down.
Do you think you would look good if you gained a little weight?

Look good? No, no way. If I gained weight... I mean, when I look in the mirror, especially at my stomach and waist, I feel like if I’m not smaller and tight-looking, then I’m just... I'm not the disciplined man I used to be on the warehouse floor. You lose that edge, you know? 

It’s like those old conveyor belts we had in the sorting facility before the remodel. They were these heavy, thick rubber belts, and over time, if they got even a little slack in them, they’d start catching on the rollers. Once a belt catches, it throws the whole line off. I remember one Tuesday, right before the holiday rush, the main line jammed up so bad it sheared the drive pin right off the motor. The maintenance guy, old man Henderson—he always smelled like peppermint and WD-40—he had to order a custom pin from this shop three towns over. Took them two days to machine the thing. We had guys standing around doing nothing for 48 hours while the freight just piled up on the dock. The regional manager came down, and he was livid, just screaming about metrics and throughput. But you can't argue with a broken motor, right? 

But yeah, if I get soft around the middle, I just... I don't look right. I have to stay tight.
Do you think you look too thin now?

Too thin? I mean, my sister keeps harping on it, and my regular doctor acts like I'm about to drop dead or something. They keep saying I'm in some kind of danger, but they're making a mountain out of a molehill. They just don't get it. I'm just keeping myself light, you know? Sharp. Ready for work. If you're hauling freight, you can't be dragging extra weight around. 

Speaking of hauling freight, we had this new guy start last week, young kid, maybe twenty-two. Showed up on his first day wearing these pristine, bright white sneakers. I took one look at him and told him those shoes wouldn't last till lunch. Sure enough, by ten o'clock he dropped a pallet jack right on his toe. Didn't break it, but the grease stain on that white mesh... ruined 'em. I always tell these kids, you gotta get steel-toe boots. I bought my Red Wings back in 2018, and they're still holding up. I get them resoled every couple of years by this cobbler downtown. Real old-school guy, his shop smells like leather polish and cigar smoke. He uses this heavy-duty stitching that you just don't see anymore. Most boots you buy off the shelf now, the soles start peeling off after six months because they just glue them on. It's cheap manufacturing, is what it is. 

But yeah, my sister and the doctor... they just don't understand that I'm just staying sharp for the floor. I'm not in any danger.
Do you think your weight is the same as other men your age and height?

Same as other guys? I don't know, I haven't really... I mean, I don't go around comparing myself to the other guys on the dock. Most of them are carrying a lot of extra baggage, if you ask me. 

Take Big Mike, for instance. We call him Big Mike because, well, the guy's built like a forklift. He must eat three meatball subs a day from that deli down on 4th Street. You know the one? They wrap the subs in that thick butcher paper, but the grease still soaks right through. Mike leaves those greasy wrappers all over the breakroom tables. It drives the janitor, Luis, absolutely crazy. Luis is this quiet guy, always listening to Spanish talk radio on his little portable speaker while he mops. He uses this industrial floor cleaner that smells like industrial pine and bleach. It's strong stuff. Actually, last winter, the heating system in the warehouse went out, and Luis accidentally left a bucket of that cleaner right by the loading bay doors. The whole bucket froze solid. We had to use a crowbar to chip it out so we could move the pallets. Took us an hour just to clear the ice. 

But yeah, I don't really pay attention to what I weigh compared to guys like Mike or anyone else. I'm just focused on my own thing.
Are you afraid of gaining weight if you eat a normal amount of food?

Yeah, I mean... afraid? It's just... if I eat a normal amount, like if I have rice or bread, or heaven forbid something greasy, I just... I can't stop thinking about it. I feel like it's just going to sit on me right away. I'll be checking the scale or pulling at my belt the next morning just to make sure I didn't let myself go. 

Speaking of belts, I've had the same leather work belt for fifteen years. It's got this heavy brass buckle that I bought at a flea market out by the old fairgrounds. You remember when they used to host that massive swap meet every summer? People would come from three states over just to sell junk out of their trunks. I bought that buckle from this guy selling vintage motorcycle parts. He had a whole table of carburetors and spark plugs, just covered in this fine layer of rust and dust. His dog, this massive Rottweiler mix, was just sleeping under the folding table the whole time. It was so hot that day, I think it was August of '09, the asphalt was literally soft under my boots. You could smell the funnel cakes from the food trucks mixing with the smell of exhaust... 

But yeah, if I eat that stuff, I just have to check the belt the next day to make sure I'm still tight. I can't afford to get soft.
Do you think your fear of gaining weight is because you believe it would change your appearance in a way that you couldn't accept?

I mean, change my appearance... yeah, I guess so. It's more about what it means, you know? When I look in the mirror, especially at my stomach and waist, I feel like... if I'm not smaller and tight-looking, then I'm just not that disciplined guy I used to be on the warehouse floor. It's about standards. 

Speaking of standards, they really lowered them when they bought those new forklifts last year. The old ones, the yellow Komatsus, those things were built like tanks. You could run them for a twelve-hour shift and they wouldn't even hiccup. The new ones are electric, which I guess is supposed to be better for the environment or whatever, but they're so quiet. It's actually a safety hazard if you ask me. Last month, Dave—he's the guy who usually works the loading dock on Tuesdays—he almost backed one right into a stack of wooden pallets because he couldn't hear the motor over the sound of the rain hitting the tin roof. We get these massive thunderstorms in the spring, the kind that just rattle the whole building. The rain comes down so hard it sounds like a thousand hammers hitting the metal. I actually love that sound. Reminds me of when I was a kid and we had this old aluminum camper trailer... 

But yeah, the mirror thing. If my waist isn't tight, it just feels like I'm losing my edge, like I'm getting soft and undisciplined. I can't let that happen.
Do you think you look the way you actually are when you look in the mirror?

Look the way I actually am? I don't really know... I mean, I'm not sure what you mean by that. A mirror's just a piece of glass, right? It just shows what's standing in front of it. 

Speaking of mirrors, though, we have these massive convex safety mirrors bolted up at all the blind intersections in the warehouse. You know the ones? The big round domes so you can see if a forklift is coming around the pallet racks. They get absolutely caked in cardboard dust. Cardboard dust is the worst thing in the world, I swear. It gets into everything—your hair, your boots, your lungs. I've been blowing my nose and seeing brown for twenty years. Anyway, management finally hired this outside crew last month to come in and wipe down all the high beams and those safety mirrors. They brought in this huge electric scissor lift that beeped every single time it moved an inch. Just this loud, piercing beep echoing off the concrete floors all shift long. It drove our dispatch guy, Gary, totally out of his mind. Gary’s already a high-strung guy, always chewing on those little plastic coffee stirrers until they're flat. He was practically screaming over the two-way radio trying to get the crew to turn the backup alarm off, but they didn't speak much English, so it was just a whole mess...

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, right, looking in the mirror. Yeah, I don't know. I just look at it and see me, I guess. I haven't really thought about it being any different from reality.
Do you think your mirror reflection accurately represents how you look to other people?

Accurately represents how I look to other people? I... I don't really know how other people see me. I mean, they probably just see a guy in work boots, right? I don't really pay attention to what they're seeing. 

Speaking of paying attention, you really have to keep your eyes peeled when you're walking across the yard at work. The delivery trucks come flying in off the access road like they're qualifying for the Daytona 500. Just last week, this guy in a flatbed hauling corrugated steel—he must have been doing forty in a fifteen zone. He locked up his brakes right by the loading dock and left these massive black skid marks on the concrete. The smell of burnt rubber just hung in the air for hours. It reminded me of this time my brother and I went to a drag strip down in Texas back in the nineties. We sat in the bleachers all afternoon drinking cheap beer out of those flimsy plastic cups that sweat all over your hands. By the end of the day, our ears were ringing so bad we had to yell at each other in the car ride home just to have a conversation. My brother had this old Ford Ranger, a manual transmission, and the clutch was slipping so bad we barely made it up the hills...

But yeah, the mirror and other people. I don't really know. I just see what I see, and they see what they see. I don't think about it too much.
Do you think there's a difference between how you see your body and how others see it?

Difference between how I see it and how others see it? Man, I couldn't tell you. People don't exactly come up to me on the warehouse floor and critique my waistline, you know? I'm not really sure what they see. 

Though, speaking of how things look, they just changed out all the overhead lights in the main sorting area last weekend. Swapped out the old buzzing fluorescents for these high-efficiency LED panels. Let me tell you, it completely messes with your eyes. Everything looks almost... blue now? It's like working in a hospital or a spaceship or something. My buddy Mike—he runs the shrink-wrap machine—he's been complaining all week that the new lights are giving him a migraine. He even brought in these tinted safety glasses, the kind guys wear when they're doing light welding, just to take the edge off. Management told him it was a safety violation because the lenses were too dark, and they got into this huge shouting match right there by the time clock. Mike’s been there thirty years, he’s not gonna take crap from some twenty-something shift supervisor who just got his degree. It was a whole scene, everyone just stopped loading the conveyor belt to watch... 

Anyway, what was the question? Oh, right, how others see my body. Yeah, I have no clue. I just keep to myself mostly, so I don't really know if they see something different than I do.
Do you think your body looks the way you think it does when you're not looking in a mirror?

When I'm not looking in a mirror? I mean, I guess it just feels like my body. I don't really sit around picturing it in my head when I'm walking around, you know? It's just... there. 

Speaking of just being there, we had this stray cat that just started hanging around the loading docks a few months ago. Little orange tabby, missing half its left ear. At first, it would just sit by the dumpsters, but then guys started leaving out pieces of their sandwiches, you know, some turkey or a little piece of cheese. Before long, that cat was practically running the place. We named him Forklift. He'd sleep on top of the pallets of shrink wrap because the plastic would hold the heat from the sun. The warehouse manager, Dave, he hated it. Said it was a health hazard or something, said we'd get cited by OSHA. He tried trapping him, but Forklift was way too smart for that. He'd just sit on top of the racking, like twenty feet up, and stare down at Dave while Dave was yelling and waving a broom. It was the funniest thing. We'd all be on our fifteen-minute break, drinking terrible breakroom coffee, just watching this standoff between a fifty-year-old man and a ten-pound cat. Eventually, Dave just gave up. I think secretly he likes the cat now, because I caught him slipping Forklift some tuna from his lunch last Tuesday...

But, uh, what did you ask? My body without a mirror? Yeah, I don't really think about it. It's just my body doing the work, moving boxes. I don't really have a picture of it in my head.
Do you think your body is actually the size and shape you believe it to be?

The size and shape I believe it to be? I... I don't know. I guess? I mean, it's just my body. I don't really know what to compare it to to say if it's actually that size.

Speaking of sizes, you wouldn't believe the mess we had yesterday with this new supplier out of Ohio. They sent us three truckloads of these custom corrugated boxes, right? Supposed to be standard 18 by 18 by 24s. But whoever programmed the cutting machine at their plant must have been asleep at the wheel, because they all came in at 17 and a half inches wide. Half an inch doesn't sound like a lot, but when you're trying to pack out these specific automotive parts that are exactly 18 inches... man, it's a nightmare. The parts were just bulging out the sides, popping the packing tape right off. We had pallets of this stuff just sitting in the staging area, completely useless. The shift supervisor was losing his mind, pacing up and down the aisles, screaming into his cell phone trying to get the supplier on the line. And of course, it was a Friday afternoon, so nobody was answering. We ended up having to shrink-wrap the whole lot of them and shove them in the back corner of the warehouse until Monday. Took up three whole bays of rack space. I swear, the quality control these days is just... it's gone right out the window. Back when I started, if you messed up an order like that, you were out of a job before lunch...

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, my body size. Yeah, I don't know. I just assume it's whatever size it is. I don't really think about if it's actually that way or not.
Do you think your body appears the same to you as it does in photographs?

Photographs? I... I don't really know. I don't take a lot of pictures, to be honest. 

Actually, speaking of cameras, corporate just overhauled the whole security system at the warehouse last month. We used to have these ancient, grainy black-and-white cameras from like, the late nineties. You could barely make out a forklift on those things, let alone a person. But they brought in these outside contractors to install these new 4K dome cameras everywhere. Every aisle, every loading dock, even by the time clocks. The IT guy, Kevin, he was showing us the live feed on his iPad down in the breakroom. It's insane, you can zoom right in from fifty feet up and read the actual barcode on a shipping label. 

Of course, all the guys on the floor are paranoid now. They think management is timing our bathroom breaks or watching to see if we take an extra two minutes for lunch. Jimmy—he drives the cherry picker—he actually took a broom handle and taped a piece of cardboard over the camera pointing at his main aisle. Said it was a "privacy shield." Well, HR didn't think it was very funny. They hauled him into the front office and gave him a final written warning for tampering with company property. The union rep had to get involved, and it was this whole big mess that dragged on for three days...

But, sorry, what did you ask me? Oh, right, photos of myself. Yeah, I avoid the camera mostly. My wife might snap a picture at Christmas or something, but I don't really look at them, so I couldn't tell you if I look the same in them or not. I just really don't know.
Do you think your body appears normal to you?

Normal? I mean... I don't know what normal really is anymore. But I know that when I look in the mirror, especially right around my stomach and my waist... I just feel like if I’m not smaller, if I don't keep it really tight-looking, then I’m just not the disciplined man I used to be on the warehouse floor. 

Speaking of discipline on the floor, I'll tell you, it is a complete joke these days. Management just brought in this new batch of summer temps last week. College kids. There's this one kid, Brayden or Jayden or something. Kid comes in wearing these spotless, expensive white sneakers and spends half his shift looking at his phone behind the forklift charging stations. I caught him on Wednesday trying to build a mixed pallet of cleaning supplies and paper goods, and I swear to you, he put the heavy liquid bleach gallons right on top of the flimsy paper towel boxes. Just completely crushed the whole bottom layer. We had fluid leaking everywhere, eating through the cardboard. Took me and another old-timer forty-five minutes to clean up the spill and re-stack the whole thing, and this kid just stood there complaining about his back hurting. His back! He’s twenty years old! When I was his age, I was throwing eighty-pound sacks of feed grain for ten hours a day and you didn't hear a peep out of me. We had pride in the work, you know? You had to be tough, you had to be disciplined. Now they just let anybody drive a high-reach without testing if they actually have a brain in their head...

But, uh, sorry, what was the question? Oh, if I look normal. Yeah, I just... I need to look disciplined. Like I can still do the work. That's all.
Do you think you are underweight?

Underweight? I don't... I mean, my sister and my regular doctor keep saying I'm in some kind of danger. They make this huge deal out of it. But they're just making it bigger than it actually is because they don't understand that I'm just keeping myself light. I need to stay sharp and ready for the work, you know? 

And speaking of being ready for work, you would not believe the absolute disaster we had with the new inventory system they rolled out on Monday. They brought in these consultants—bunch of guys in suits who have probably never lifted a box in their lives—and they replaced our old barcode scanners with these new touchscreen tablets that strap to your forearm. Sounds real futuristic, right? Well, the batteries on these things die after like, four hours. So right in the middle of the afternoon rush, half the floor is suddenly flying blind. We had three trucks from the Midwest waiting at the docks, drivers getting ticked off because they're on a tight schedule, and we can't scan a single pallet onto the trucks. So we had to go back to the old paper manifests. Doing it by hand! Half the guys don't even know how to read the old grid codes anymore because they rely so much on the computers. I had to walk up and down the loading bays, literally pointing out which skids went to which truck, just to keep the line moving. It took us until eight o'clock at night to clear the backlog, and the terminal manager was furious about the overtime pay. If they had just listened to the guys who actually do the work instead of some fancy tech company... 

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, I'm not in danger or anything. I just keep myself light so I can move fast on the floor. That's all it is.
Do you think your fear of gaining weight is because you have a distorted view of what you look like?

Distorted view? I... I don't think it's distorted. It's just that I know exactly how my body reacts. If I eat rice, or bread, or anything greasy at all, I can't stop thinking about how it's just going to sit on me right away. It's like I can feel it turning into fat immediately. I have to check the scale or my belt the next morning just to make sure I didn't let myself go. 

Speaking of letting things go, you should see the state of the breakroom refrigerators at work. It is an absolute biohazard in there. People just leave their Tupperware in there for weeks, sometimes months. Last Friday, the maintenance guy, Hector, decided he'd finally had enough and did a total cleanout. He found a container of what used to be chili that had literally grown this thick, fuzzy green mold all over it. It looked like a science experiment. And the smell when he opened the lid... I swear, half the warehouse smelled like a dead animal for the rest of the shift. Hector was gagging, trying to double-bag it in those heavy-duty contractor trash bags. He ended up just throwing the whole plastic container away because there was no saving it. And then, of course, on Monday, this guy from shipping, Gary, starts throwing a massive fit because his "good" Tupperware is missing. He went right to the shift supervisor demanding the company reimburse him for a five-dollar piece of plastic he abandoned a month ago. The nerve of some people, I swear. If you can't be disciplined enough to clean up after yourself...

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, the weight thing. Yeah, I just... I check my belt because I can't afford to get soft. That's all.
Do you think your weight is the same as what you see in the mirror?

Well, the mirror... I mean, I see myself as lean, you know? Like I'm just stripped down, ready to work, quick on my feet. But the numbers on the scale... I'm only even here talking to you because the medical clinic for the logistics company wouldn't clear me for duty. They said my weight was too low to pass the physical. 

And don't even get me started on those company physicals. It's a complete racket. They send you to this strip-mall clinic out on Route 9, right? You sit in this waiting room with fluorescent lights that buzz so loud it gives you a migraine, sitting on chairs from the 1980s. Last time I was there, the guy next to me was a long-haul driver trying to renew his DOT card, and he was hacking up a lung the whole time. Sounded like a diesel engine trying to turn over in sub-zero weather. And the doctor they have doing the exams... this guy looked like he was about eighty-five years old. He took my blood pressure with one of those old manual cuffs, pumped it up so tight I thought my hand was going to fall off, and then he just stared at the wall for like two minutes while the air hissed out. I swear he fell asleep with the stethoscope in his ears. Then he makes me do a hearing test in a booth that smelled like stale coffee and mothballs. The whole thing took three hours just so they could stamp a piece of paper saying I can lift fifty pounds, which I've been doing every single day for thirty years without their permission. 

But, uh, what was the question? Oh, right, the mirror and the weight. Yeah, the clinic says the number is too low, but when I look in the mirror, I just see a guy who's lean and ready to get back on the floor. That's all.

target_item.name: Restrictive_Intake
target_item.manifestation: Most days I keep it to black coffee, maybe a boiled egg or a little tuna, and if I’m not moving freight on a shift I tell myself I don’t need a real meal anyway.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about limiting what I eat, which directly corresponds to the Restrictive_Intake symptom regarding restricting energy intake.

patient.answer:
Well, I guess... yeah, I keep things pretty tight. Most days I just stick to black coffee, maybe a boiled egg or a little bit of tuna. If I'm not actually on the floor moving freight, I just tell myself I don't really need a real meal anyway. You don't need the fuel if the engine ain't running, right? 

Speaking of engines, my buddy Carl—he works over at the auto parts distribution center across town—he was telling me about this whole shipment of alternators they got in last month. Apparently, they were all defective straight from the manufacturer. Just totally shot. Carl said they had to load 'em all back onto the pallets, wrap 'em up, and ship 'em right back to Mexico. The shrink wrap they use over there is garbage, though. It's that thin, cheap stuff that tears if you even look at it funny. I always tell our purchasing guy to buy the heavy-duty wrap, the 80-gauge stuff. It costs a few cents more a roll, but it saves you hours of re-wrapping when a pallet shifts in transit. I remember one time we had a whole skid of windshield washer fluid tip over inside a trailer because some rookie used the cheap wrap. Blue liquid everywhere. Smelled like windex for a month. 

But yeah, I just... I don't eat much. Just keep it light so I don't get weighed down.

doctor.intent: determine if patient's fear of gaining weight is associated with a distorted body image
doctor.question: Do you think you would look good if you gained a little weight?

target_item.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: When I look in the mirror, especially at my stomach and waist, I feel like if I’m not smaller and tight-looking then I’m not the disciplined man I used to be on the warehouse floor.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question asks if the patient thinks they would look good if they gained a little weight, which directly relates to how the patient evaluates their body image, weight, and shape.

patient.answer:
Look good? No, no way. If I gained weight... I mean, when I look in the mirror, especially at my stomach and waist, I feel like if I’m not smaller and tight-looking, then I’m just... I'm not the disciplined man I used to be on the warehouse floor. You lose that edge, you know? 

It’s like those old conveyor belts we had in the sorting facility before the remodel. They were these heavy, thick rubber belts, and over time, if they got even a little slack in them, they’d start catching on the rollers. Once a belt catches, it throws the whole line off. I remember one Tuesday, right before the holiday rush, the main line jammed up so bad it sheared the drive pin right off the motor. The maintenance guy, old man Henderson—he always smelled like peppermint and WD-40—he had to order a custom pin from this shop three towns over. Took them two days to machine the thing. We had guys standing around doing nothing for 48 hours while the freight just piled up on the dock. The regional manager came down, and he was livid, just screaming about metrics and throughput. But you can't argue with a broken motor, right? 

But yeah, if I get soft around the middle, I just... I don't look right. I have to stay tight.

Too thin? I mean, my sister keeps harping on it, and my regular doctor acts like I'm about to drop dead or something. They keep saying I'm in some kind of danger, but they're making a mountain out of a molehill. They just don't get it. I'm just keeping myself light, you know? Sharp. Ready for work. If you're hauling freight, you can't be dragging extra weight around. 

Speaking of hauling freight, we had this new guy start last week, young kid, maybe twenty-two. Showed up on his first day wearing these pristine, bright white sneakers. I took one look at him and told him those shoes wouldn't last till lunch. Sure enough, by ten o'clock he dropped a pallet jack right on his toe. Didn't break it, but the grease stain on that white mesh... ruined 'em. I always tell these kids, you gotta get steel-toe boots. I bought my Red Wings back in 2018, and they're still holding up. I get them resoled every couple of years by this cobbler downtown. Real old-school guy, his shop smells like leather polish and cigar smoke. He uses this heavy-duty stitching that you just don't see anymore. Most boots you buy off the shelf now, the soles start peeling off after six months because they just glue them on. It's cheap manufacturing, is what it is. 

But yeah, my sister and the doctor... they just don't understand that I'm just staying sharp for the floor. I'm not in any danger.

Same as other guys? I don't know, I haven't really... I mean, I don't go around comparing myself to the other guys on the dock. Most of them are carrying a lot of extra baggage, if you ask me. 

Take Big Mike, for instance. We call him Big Mike because, well, the guy's built like a forklift. He must eat three meatball subs a day from that deli down on 4th Street. You know the one? They wrap the subs in that thick butcher paper, but the grease still soaks right through. Mike leaves those greasy wrappers all over the breakroom tables. It drives the janitor, Luis, absolutely crazy. Luis is this quiet guy, always listening to Spanish talk radio on his little portable speaker while he mops. He uses this industrial floor cleaner that smells like industrial pine and bleach. It's strong stuff. Actually, last winter, the heating system in the warehouse went out, and Luis accidentally left a bucket of that cleaner right by the loading bay doors. The whole bucket froze solid. We had to use a crowbar to chip it out so we could move the pallets. Took us an hour just to clear the ice. 

But yeah, I don't really pay attention to what I weigh compared to guys like Mike or anyone else. I'm just focused on my own thing.

Yeah, I mean... afraid? It's just... if I eat a normal amount, like if I have rice or bread, or heaven forbid something greasy, I just... I can't stop thinking about it. I feel like it's just going to sit on me right away. I'll be checking the scale or pulling at my belt the next morning just to make sure I didn't let myself go. 

Speaking of belts, I've had the same leather work belt for fifteen years. It's got this heavy brass buckle that I bought at a flea market out by the old fairgrounds. You remember when they used to host that massive swap meet every summer? People would come from three states over just to sell junk out of their trunks. I bought that buckle from this guy selling vintage motorcycle parts. He had a whole table of carburetors and spark plugs, just covered in this fine layer of rust and dust. His dog, this massive Rottweiler mix, was just sleeping under the folding table the whole time. It was so hot that day, I think it was August of '09, the asphalt was literally soft under my boots. You could smell the funnel cakes from the food trucks mixing with the smell of exhaust... 

But yeah, if I eat that stuff, I just have to check the belt the next day to make sure I'm still tight. I can't afford to get soft.

Speaking of standards, they really lowered them when they bought those new forklifts last year. The old ones, the yellow Komatsus, those things were built like tanks. You could run them for a twelve-hour shift and they wouldn't even hiccup. The new ones are electric, which I guess is supposed to be better for the environment or whatever, but they're so quiet. It's actually a safety hazard if you ask me. Last month, Dave—he's the guy who usually works the loading dock on Tuesdays—he almost backed one right into a stack of wooden pallets because he couldn't hear the motor over the sound of the rain hitting the tin roof. We get these massive thunderstorms in the spring, the kind that just rattle the whole building. The rain comes down so hard it sounds like a thousand hammers hitting the metal. I actually love that sound. Reminds me of when I was a kid and we had this old aluminum camper trailer... 

But yeah, the mirror thing. If my waist isn't tight, it just feels like I'm losing my edge, like I'm getting soft and undisciplined. I can't let that happen.

Look the way I actually am? I don't really know... I mean, I'm not sure what you mean by that. A mirror's just a piece of glass, right? It just shows what's standing in front of it.

Anyway, management finally hired this outside crew last month to come in and wipe down all the high beams and those safety mirrors. They brought in this huge electric scissor lift that beeped every single time it moved an inch. Just this loud, piercing beep echoing off the concrete floors all shift long. It drove our dispatch guy, Gary, totally out of his mind. Gary’s already a high-strung guy, always chewing on those little plastic coffee stirrers until they're flat. He was practically screaming over the two-way radio trying to get the crew to turn the backup alarm off, but they didn't speak much English, so it was just a whole mess...

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, right, looking in the mirror. Yeah, I don't know. I just look at it and see me, I guess. I haven't really thought about it being any different from reality.

When I'm not looking in a mirror? I mean, I guess it just feels like my body. I don't really sit around picturing it in my head when I'm walking around, you know? It's just... there.

He'd just sit on top of the racking, like twenty feet up, and stare down at Dave while Dave was yelling and waving a broom. It was the funniest thing. I think secretly he likes the cat now, because I caught him slipping Forklift some tuna from his lunch last Tuesday...

But, uh, what did you ask? My body without a mirror? Yeah, I don't really think about it. It's just my body doing the work, moving boxes. I don't really have a picture of it in my head.

patient.answer:
Well, the mirror... I mean, I see myself as lean, you know? Like I'm just stripped down, ready to work, quick on my feet. But the numbers on the scale... I'm only even here talking to you because the medical clinic for the logistics company wouldn't clear me for duty. They said my weight was too low to pass the physical. 

And don't even get me started on those company physicals. It's a complete racket. They send you to this strip-mall clinic out on Route 9, right? You sit in this waiting room with fluorescent lights that buzz so loud it gives you a migraine, sitting on chairs from the 1980s. Last time I was there, the guy next to me was a long-haul driver trying to renew his DOT card, and he was hacking up a lung the whole time. Sounded like a diesel engine trying to turn over in sub-zero weather. And the doctor they have doing the exams... this guy looked like he was about eighty-five years old. He took my blood pressure with one of those old manual cuffs, pumped it up so tight I thought my hand was going to fall off, and then he just stared at the wall for like two minutes while the air hissed out. I swear he fell asleep with the stethoscope in his ears. Then he makes me do a hearing test in a booth that smelled like stale coffee and mothballs. The whole thing took three hours just so they could stamp a piece of paper saying I can lift fifty pounds, which I've been doing every single day for thirty years without their permission. 

But, uh, what was the question? Oh, right, the mirror and the weight. Yeah, the clinic says the number is too low, but when I look in the mirror, I just see a guy who's lean and ready to get back on the floor. That's all.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a distorted body image and an intense fear of gaining weight, which leads to restrictive eating habits. Despite being underweight, the patient perceives themselves as 'lean' and 'ready to work,' indicating a significant discrepancy between their self-perception and reality.
